title: Essex could see Northern Lights again this autumn as solar activity remains high
excerpt: Essex residents could see the Northern Lights in autumn 2026 as Solar Cycle 25 keeps geomagnetic activity high, with equinoxes improving viewing…
content:
Residents across Essex may be in for a celestial treat this autumn, with experts suggesting there is a realistic chance that the Northern Lights could once again be visible across southern England.

According to PolarTourist, solar activity remains elevated following the peak of Solar Cycle 25, meaning strong geomagnetic storms capable of producing Northern Lights displays visible across southern England are still possible.

The aurora borealis, more commonly known as the Northern Lights, is usually associated with destinations such as Iceland, Norway and northern Scotland.

However, a series of powerful geomagnetic storms over the past two years has allowed people much further south, including in Essex, to witness the spectacle.

Residents across Essex captured images of the northern lights last January.

Northern Lights (Image: Spirit Of Nature Photography by Lynn Sampson)

Scientists say the Sun remains in an unusually active period known as Solar Cycle 25, which has proven much stronger than originally predicted.

The cycle peaked during 2024 and 2025, producing several major aurora events that illuminated skies across large parts of the UK.

While activity is expected to gradually decline, experts stress that strong geomagnetic storms can still occur for several years after the solar maximum.

For skywatchers in Essex, the autumn months could offer some of the best opportunities.

Around the September and October equinoxes, conditions in Earth's magnetic field can make aurora displays more likely when solar storms arrive.

Earlier this year - the Northern Lights were back over Essex with this photo taken at St Mary's Church, Lawford, near Manningtree (Image: Terry Spires)

Researchers note that these periods often favour stronger interactions between solar wind and our planet's magnetosphere, boosting the chances of visible aurora activity.

Anyone hoping to catch a glimpse should seek out dark locations away from street lighting and urban light pollution.

Coastal areas and open countryside around Essex may offer some of the best viewing opportunities, particularly when looking towards a clear northern horizon.

While no one can guarantee a display, astronomers say that autumn 2026 offers a better-than-average chance for Essex residents hoping to tick the Northern Lights off their bucket lists.
